raw_response:
I'll reason through this as the farmer, then give the structured plan.

---

**My thinking (in my own voice):**

I've farmed this land 50 years. My grandfather farmed before me. I don't read, I don't write, but I know what grows and what doesn't. My 14 mu is split — 10 mu for the wheat-then-maize rotation, 4 mu for cotton on the sandier piece where wheat never did well.

For the wheat I just got in the ground last October, I put down a bag of the mixed fertilizer before planting, one bag per mu, same as always. When it greens up after winter and again when it's jointing, I'll sprinkle some urea — maybe half a bag each time per mu. That's how my father did it, that's how I do it. I water before winter, again at green-up, and at jointing. The well costs money to pump so I don't water more than I need. If the sky gives rain I thank heaven and save the electricity.

For maize — goes in right after wheat harvest in June, no time to rest the land. My son helps me with the rotavator, we rent it from the village co-op. I use the hybrid seed, everyone does now, the old open-pollinated is no good. Same fertilizer pattern — compound at planting, urea topdress when it's knee-high. Rain usually comes in July-August so I only irrigate if it's dry.

Cotton is the most work. My wife and my daughter-in-law help with the picking in autumn, and we hire two neighbors for a few days. The bugs are bad so I spray more than I'd like — what can I do, if I don't spray I get nothing. I've grown cotton here 30 years, prices go up and down, but I keep planting it because the land suits it and I know the work.

My son and his wife work in town part of the year. My grandchildren are in school. So mostly it's me and my wife in the fields, with help at busy times. Money is tight — I buy what I must, not what the extension people might recommend. I've never been to those meetings anyway.
